sources.citation: Newman, Paul. 1969. Linguistic relationship, language shifting, and historical inference. Afrika und Übersee 53: 217-223. (Open CC BY 4.0 copy in IUScholarWorks, Paul Newman Papers, hdl 2022/21300.)
sources.note: Nothing. Ethnohistorical paper on seven Tera-speaking villages near Bima Hill and documented language shifts (Bolewa->Tera at Deba/Kinafa, Tera->Bolewa at Kwamu/Kafarati, Tera->Bura at Kwaya-Tera, Kanakuru->'Pidlimndi dialect of Tera' at Walama); linguistic evidence deferred to Newman & Ma 1966 (fn. 6). The names Jara/Jera do not occur; no phonology, tone, stress or accent content.

sources.citation: Newman, Paul. 1977. Chadic classification and reconstructions. Afroasiatic Linguistics 5(1): 1-42.
sources.note: Basis for placing Jara in the Tera group (cited by Gravina 2014); may indicate the source of Newman's Jara data. Comparative, not a phonology.

sources.citation: Newman, Paul & Roxana Ma. 1966. Comparative Chadic: phonology and lexicon. Journal of African Languages 5(3): 218-251.
sources.note: Explicitly excludes tone for all languages: symbol footnote 'vowel length is indicated for Hausa and Tera forms only. Tone is nowhere indicated.'; conclusion: 'much research needs to be done on vowels, tone, and syntax.' About 15 Jara forms are cited untoned (ndomox 'sheep', ndəra 'moon', vaɗa 'four', pərum 'knee'..), and item 94 notes 'The /s/ in closely related Jara (3c) shows that the voicing of the spirant in Tera (3e) is an innovation.' No stress or tone statement for Jara.
